title: Scientists Borrow a Superpower from Wrinkly, Cancer-Proof Mole Rats—and Give It to Mice!
summary: Imagine an animal that's about the size of a mouse but can live longer than a pet cat—up to 41 years! That's the naked mole rat, a wrinkly, pink rodent that scientists love to study. Why? Because these little guys almost never get cancer, and they stay healthy way into old age. Now, researchers have taken one of their secret weapons and given it to regular mice. The secret is a gooey molecule called high molecular weight hyaluronic acid, or HMW-HA (say "hi-a-lur-on-ic acid"). Naked mole rats have about ten times more of it than mice or humans. It's like a protective shield that fights inflammation (swelling that can damage your body) and stops tumors from growing. Scientists at the University of Rochester found the gene that makes this shield in mole rats. They carefully added that gene to mouse DNA. The result? The new mice had more HMW-HA, got fewer cancers, had less inflammation in their guts and other tissues, and lived about 4.4% longer than normal mice. That might not sound like a lot, but it's a huge deal. It proves that a longevity trick from one animal can work in another. Next, the team wants to see if this could help humans stay healthier as we age. "Our next goal is to transfer this benefit to humans," says lead researcher Vera Gorbunova. Who knew a wrinkly little rodent could hold clues to a longer, healthier life?
why_it_matters: Understanding how mole rats stay cancer-free could lead to medicines that keep you and your family healthier as you grow older.

background_read: Naked mole rats are burrowing rodents from East Africa that live in large underground colonies, similar to ants or bees.
Hyaluronic acid is a natural substance in our skin, and many face creams include it to keep skin plump and hydrated.
Vera Gorbunova (a biologist at the University of Rochester, a university in the United States) has been studying why mole rats stay cancer-free for over 20 years.
Article_Structure: WHO: Naked mole rats, which have a special molecule called HMW-HA that protects them.
WHAT: Scientists transferred the gene for HMW-HA into mice, making them healthier and giving them longer lives.
WHERE: Research done at the University of Rochester in the USA.
WHY: To understand how animals resist aging and cancer, hoping to one day help humans stay healthier as they grow old.

perspectives.description: If this works in humans, it could lead to pills that slow aging and reduce cancer, giving people more healthy years.
Genetically altering animals can have side effects; we must carefully test if it is safe for people.
This is still early research in mice, and many anti-aging treatments that work in rodents fail later in human trials.
